subject: physics
title: Nuclear fission
key_idea: (Separate science) In **nuclear fission** a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei. Energy and two or three neutrons are released. The neutrons can start a **chain reaction**, which a reactor controls to make electricity.

blocks.text: (Separate science) Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, such as uranium-235 or plutonium. It is one nuclear reaction that can be a source of energy. This section covers the process step by step.

items.meaning: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei.
Neutrons from one fission are absorbed by other nuclei, which split and release more neutrons.

items.text: The unstable nucleus first absorbs a **neutron**.
It splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.
Two or three neutrons are released, as well as gamma rays, and energy.

items: All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
The products of fission are radioactive.
Fission without a neutron being absorbed (spontaneous fission) is rare.
Each fission releases more than one neutron.
Each neutron can be absorbed by another nucleus, which then splits.
In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is **controlled**.
In a nuclear weapon the chain reaction is **uncontrolled**, which causes an explosion.
A nucleus absorbs a neutron, splits into two parts and releases two or three neutrons, gamma rays and energy.
The neutrons can start a chain reaction.
A controlled chain reaction is used in a reactor. An uncontrolled one causes a nuclear explosion.

blocks.text: (Separate science) A reactor keeps the chain reaction going at a steady rate. These parts control it.

rows: Nuclei absorb neutrons and split, releasing energy.
Slows down the neutrons, so they are more likely to be absorbed and cause fission.
Absorb neutrons. Pushed in, they leave fewer neutrons for the chain reaction, so fewer fissions.
Carries the thermal energy away from the reactor.

items: Pull the control rods out and more neutrons are available, so the reaction speeds up.
Push the control rods in and fewer neutrons are available, so the reaction slows down.

diagram.alt: Energy flows from the fission fragments to the coolant, to steam, to a turbine and then to electricity.
steps: Thermal energy transferred to the coolant

items: The moderator slows neutrons. Control rods absorb neutrons.
Moving the control rods changes the rate of energy release.
Kinetic energy of the fission products becomes thermal energy, which makes steam to turn a turbine.

sections.heading: Energy from fission and the arguments for and against

blocks.text: (Separate science) Each fission releases a tiny amount of energy. A reactor needs a huge number of fissions each second.

blocks.label: Energy released
blocks.formula: energy released = number of fissions × energy released per fission
where: number of fissions in one second (a number)
energy released per fission in joules (J)

diagram.alt: Calculate the energy released each second by a reactor.
diagram.question: In a reactor there are {n} × 10¹⁷ fission reactions each second. Each reaction releases 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Calculate the energy released in 1 second, in megajoules (MJ).

blocks.text: Nuclear power: arguments for and against

items: For: no carbon dioxide is produced, so it does not add to global warming.
For: a large power output from a small amount of fuel, and it saves fossil fuels.
For: low running costs once the power station is built.
Against: **radioactive waste** stays dangerous for a long time and must be stored safely.
Against: expensive to build and to decommission.
Against: the risk of an accident, which could expose people to radiation or contaminate an area.
Against: public worry about safety, waste and terrorism.
Energy released = number of fissions × energy per fission.
Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide and has a large output.
Waste, cost and the risk of an accident are the main arguments against.

checks.q: Describe the process of nuclear fission.
checks.a: A neutron is absorbed by a large nucleus. The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei. Energy (and gamma rays) are released, and two or three neutrons.

checks.q: Explain how pushing the control rods further into a reactor slows down the chain reaction.
checks.a: The control rods absorb neutrons, so fewer neutrons are available for the chain reaction, so there are fewer fissions.

checks.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using nuclear power to generate electricity.
checks.a: Advantage: any one from no carbon dioxide produced, small quantities of fuel needed, fuel readily available. Disadvantage: any one from radioactive waste is produced, expensive to build, risk of an accident.

mistakes.wrong: An atom absorbs a neutron and the atom splits in two.
mistakes.right: A description in terms of only atoms loses the first two marks. Say a nucleus absorbs a neutron and the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei.

mistakes.wrong: A uranium nucleus absorbs a proton, and X-rays are released.
mistakes.right: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron. The electromagnetic radiation released is gamma rays.

worked_example.question: Nuclear fission releases energy. Describe the process of nuclear fission inside a nuclear reactor.
answer_points: A neutron is absorbed by a uranium nucleus.
The nucleus splits into two parts.
Two or three neutrons are released.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. An atom splitting into two parts can score if the first point is not given.

mistakes.wrong: The control rods slow down the neutrons.
mistakes.right: The moderator slows down the neutrons. The control rods absorb neutrons.

mistakes.wrong: Pushing the control rods in slows down the chain reaction.
mistakes.right: This is ignored as it only repeats the question. Explain that the rods absorb neutrons, so fewer neutrons are available for the chain reaction.

mistakes.wrong: Using nuclear fuel produces carbon dioxide as a harmful waste product.

worked_example.question: The energy released in a single uranium fission is very small. In a nuclear power station, the fission of uranium in the reactor releases large amounts of energy, enough to generate electricity for thousands of homes. The demand for electricity varies. Explain how large amounts of energy can be released in the reactor, and how the rate of energy release is controlled as the demand for electricity varies.
answer_points: Chain reaction: neutrons emitted in one fission go on to hit other U-235 nuclei and cause a chain reaction.
Control rods absorb, capture or stop neutrons.
This limits the number of fissions, which varies the rate of thermal energy released.
Moderator: it slows down the neutrons, which makes them more likely to cause fission.
worked_example.tip: Level-marked. For the top level, give detail on two of chain reaction, control rods and moderator, and mention the third.

worked_example.question: A nuclear power station uses fission to produce electricity. The total power output of the nuclear power station is 1.0 GW. The average power output of one fission reaction is 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ W. Calculate the number of fission reactions that occur per second. Use the equation: number of fission reactions per second = total power output ÷ average power output per fission reaction.
worked_example.tip: Missing the GW to W conversion loses a mark: 3.1 × 10ⁿ with the wrong power of ten scores 2 marks.
